summary: Extends PPP over Ethernet with two optional features: credit-based flow control and a link quality metric report. They help when PPPoE runs over links with changing bandwidth and little buffering, such as mobile point-to-point radio links. It is informational, not a standard.

plainLanguage.summary: This document adds two optional features to PPP over Ethernet. One lets each side say how much data the other side may send right now, so that a slow radio link is not overrun. The other lets a radio report how good its link is, so the router can pick a better path.

subtitle: Optional PPPoE extensions that add credit-based flow control and link quality reports for radio links whose bandwidth keeps changing.

tldr.problem: PPPoE works well when both ends have similar, steady bandwidth and buffering. Mobile point-to-point radio links have variable bandwidth and limited buffering, so a fast sender can overrun them.
tldr.mechanism: A peer grants the other side credits, and the other side may only send PPP payload while it holds credits. A separate quality packet (PADQ) reports metrics such as data rate, latency and relative link quality to the router.
tldr.outcome: Both features are optional. The IESG note says the PPP Extensions working group had reservations about the approach and advises implementors to use standard IP routing instead of split termination.

today: RFC 5578 is an Informational document that obsoletes RFC 4938, and no later RFC is listed as replacing or updating it. The IESG note in it records that the PPP Extensions Working Group had reservations about the feature and advises implementors to use standard IP routing instead of split termination.

sections.title: Introduction: The Radio Case
sections.content:
PPP over Ethernet is a protocol for establishing and encapsulating sessions between hosts, which this document calls clients, and traffic-access aggregators, which it calls servers, for PPP transport over real or emulated Ethernet. PPPoE works well when both session endpoints have similar bandwidth, forwarding and buffering capabilities that do not vary over time. Improvements can be made for applications with variable bandwidth and limited buffering, and this document addresses them with optional extensions supporting credit-based session flow control and session-based link metric quality reports.

The extensions are designed to support radio systems that exhibit point-to-point waveforms. When the local radio detects a remote radio neighbour, it initiates a PPPoE session with its local router and establishes a radio link connection with the remote radio over the point-to-point radio frequency link. The remote radio does the same with its own router, and the two radios associate the two PPPoE sessions with the radio link protocol, creating a complete data path. A PPP session is then established through the PPP IP Control Protocol, and the exchange of IP addresses lets each router insert the remote IP address into its local routing tables; the radio IP information is not inserted.

The capabilities of the radio links vary over time because of mobility, environmental conditions and changes in the waveforms and encoding, so the radio may periodically generate link quality metrics for the router, which uses them to update route costs and influence route selection. The influence on the routing protocols is beyond the scope of the document.

The IESG note in the memo records that the PPP Extensions Working Group had reservations about the desirability of the feature, because it solves a general problem at an inappropriate layer and may have unpredictable interactions with higher and lower level protocols. The techniques are intended for a deployment with a PPP termination separated from a radio termination by an Ethernet, with radio-side flow control for a slower PPP-only link to remote nodes, and implementors are better advised to avoid split termination with inter-media protocol translation and to use standard Internet Protocol routing instead.
sections.plainLanguage: PPPoE works when both ends are equally fast and never change. Radio links are neither, so a fast sender can bury a slow receiver. The memo adds a way to pace the sending side, but the working group that reviews such documents did not think it belonged in PPPoE at all.

sections.title: The Four New TLVs
sections.content:
The extensions consist of optional TLVs, that is, Type-Length-Value fields, and enhanced and newly defined discovery packets. Four new TLVs are defined: the Credits TLV with value 0x0106, the Metrics TLV with value 0x0107, the Sequence Number TLV with value 0x0108 and the Credit Scale Factor TLV with value 0x0109.

The Credits TLV contains the Forward Credit Notification and the Backward Credit Notification. The FCN represents the number of credits being granted by the local node to the peer node, and the BCN represents the number of credits remaining at the local node that were granted by the peer node. Both range from 0 to 65535. The TLV is optional with the discovery request and session-confirmation packets and required in the two new grant packets, and it may optionally be carried in the PPPoE data payload packet of the PPP stage. These fields are transmitted in network byte order.

The Metrics TLV reports link quality parameters and is required with the quality packet. It holds Resources, a percentage from 0 to 100 for the amount of remaining or available resources such as battery power, where 100 should be reported if the value cannot be calculated; Relative Link Quality, a non-dimensional number from 0 to 100 where 100 represents a link of the highest quality; a Receive-only bit indicating whether the link is bi-directional or receive-only; two bits for the scale of the Current Datarate and two for the scale of the Maximum Datarate, where the default scale is kbit/s and the others are Mbit/s, Gbit/s and Tbit/s; the Current Datarate itself, which must be less than or equal to the Maximum Datarate; Latency, the transmission delay a packet encounters, reported in absolute milliseconds and 0 if it cannot be calculated; and the Maximum Datarate, the maximum theoretical rate the link is capable of providing. When metrics are reported, both the Current Datarate and the Maximum Datarate must be reported.

The Sequence Number TLV carries a unique 16-bit sequence number to identify a specific request and the response to it. It should start at zero and be incremented by one for each new request, with the same number repeated for a retransmission. The Credit Scale Factor TLV holds the scale factor applied to the session credit calculations, and can be used to change from the default 64-byte credit unit during the discovery exchange. Its value can range from 1 byte to 65535 bytes; a zero value is ignored and the 64-byte default remains. The scale factor is set for each payload flow separately, that is, peer-to-local and local-to-peer, and once the session is established with specified scale factors, they cannot be changed.
sections.plainLanguage: Everything new is carried in small blocks of data called TLVs, each with a type number. One of them carries the credit counts, one carries the link measurements, one carries a request number so that a reply can be matched to it, and one carries the unit that the credit counts are counted in.

sections.title: Discovery Packets: Grant, Response and Quality
sections.content:
The specifications of the discovery request and session-confirmation packets are extended to include the optional Credits TLV and the Credit Scale Factor TLV, and three new discovery stage packets are defined: the session-grant, the session-credit response and the quality packet.

The request packet may contain a single Credits TLV indicating that the client asks for credit flow control for the session, with the FCN giving the initial credits granted to the server by the client and the BCN set to 0 because the client has not yet been granted credits. The server must echo the Credit Scale Factor TLV in its confirmation response to confirm the scaling and to designate the server's own factor.

The session-grant packet is new. The local node may send it at any time after the request and confirmation exchange to grant incremental credits to a peer, with a code field of 0x0A and the session identifier of the PPPoE session. Each credit corresponds to an amount of PPP payload that can be sent or received: with the default 64-byte factor, 128 bytes of payload consumes 2 credits and 130 bytes consumes 3, because credit calculations must be rounded up. The grant packet must contain a single Credits TLV and a single Sequence Number TLV. A value between 1 and 0xffff in the FCN is an incremental grant, and a value of 0x0000 is a NULL grant meaning no additional credits. The largest number of incremental credits at any time is 0xffff, and once a credit has been granted it must be honored. The BCN carries the remaining absolute credits that the peer granted to the local node, and when the local node exhausts that count it must stop transmitting payload packets.

The peer answers a grant with a session-credit response packet, with a code field of 0x0B, which carries the accumulated credit counts and the same sequence number. The quality packet, with a code field of 0x0C, may be sent at any time to query or report link quality metrics and must carry a single Metrics TLV; setting the length of that TLV to zero makes it a query. When PPP streams are carried over wireless links through radio modems, the quality of the radio link directly affects throughput, and the router uses the metrics to update route costs.
sections.plainLanguage: When one side wants the other to send more data, it sends a grant packet. The other side replies with a packet that confirms how much credit is left. A third packet type carries the measurements of the radio link, and can also be used to ask for them.

sections.title: Credit Accounting in the Session Stage
sections.content:
Credit grants exchanged in the discovery stage are referred to as out-of-band, and credit grants exchanged in the PPP session stage are referred to as in-band. Credit accounting applies only to packets transmitted in the PPP session stage. Out-of-band credit management is handled by the periodic exchange of the grant and credit response packets. In-band credit management allows credits to be granted incrementally with each PPP session stage packet; these grants are not explicitly acknowledged but are reflected in the credit flow from the peer, which offers the greatest credit-granting efficiency when traffic rates are high.

Once agreed during the discovery stage, credit grants are required to transmit packets in the PPP session stage, and a node must grant credits to its peer before the peer can transmit packets to it. Grants received from a peer are added to a local running credit counter, the accumulated credits are decremented with each packet the node transmits, and when the counter reaches zero the node must stop transmitting packets to the peer. To manage the credits it has granted, a node keeps its own running counter, which is decremented with each session stage packet received from the peer; when it reaches zero, no additional packets are expected, and the node incrementally grants more credits to keep the flow going. Packets received when the granted credits have been exhausted are discarded.

The session stage extensions define the optional use of the Credits TLV, called an in-band credit grant. The first field after the session stage length must be checked: if it equals the PPP protocol identifier 0xc021, normal payload processing occurs; otherwise a TLV is assumed and its length is subtracted from the overall payload length.

The memo also covers retransmission. When a node does not receive a credit response within a specified time, it should transmit a new grant packet with zero credits, using the same sequence number and doubling the waiting period. The reply indicates whether the previously granted credits were accumulated, and if they were not, a grant with credits and an incremented sequence number should be sent. A node may also generate quality packets on its own, though the rate should be throttled so as not to overrun the peer, and the sending and receiving of discovery packets are independent of credit counts, so a node must always be able to receive a grant and send a response.
sections.plainLanguage: Each side keeps a counter of how much the other side may still send. Every packet sent uses credit, and when the counter reaches zero the sender has to stop and wait for more credit to be granted. Credits can be handed over with the data itself or in separate packets.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The memo defines a mechanism for adding flow control to existing PPP over Ethernet sessions. The extensions come after the existing PPPoE security mechanisms described in RFC 2516, and it is required that the Service TLV and the session identifier always be validated before credits are processed.

The IANA considerations record that four PPPoE TLV values and three PPPoE code fields have been assigned for this document: TLV values 262 to 265 for Credits, Metrics, Sequence Number and Credit Scale Factor, and code fields 10, 11 and 12 for the session-grant, session-credit response and quality packets.
sections.plainLanguage: The new packets carry the same kind of protection as the rest of PPPoE, and a node must check which session a packet belongs to before it acts on the credit counts in it.
